intro.heading: You cannot gather carers who are never in the same place.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A home care manager changes how the service records a refused medication visit. She holds two short briefings at the office, one at nine and one at four, to catch as many carers as she can. Eleven come. Nineteen are out on rounds, and five more are on a different patch across the county. She posts the new steps to the team and asks everyone to read them. Weeks later she cannot say who read it, who understood it, or what a carer will actually do when a client says no at the door. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: The manager changes the steps for a refused medication visit.
Two office briefings are held, at nine and at four.
Eleven carers attend. The new steps go out to everyone else.
Nineteen carers were on rounds. Nobody can say who has seen the steps.
A few carers replied "thanks". A reply is not understanding.
Five carers across the county rarely come in. They learn from each other in the car park.
Eleven signatures and a pile of thumbs up. Nothing about the other nineteen.
“What do you do if a client refuses their medication?” The answer depends on who is asked.

trail_close: Domiciliary care is delivered out of sight, one home at a time. The training follow up has to reach a carer where she actually is, which is usually on a doorstep with a phone in her hand.

why.heading: When nobody shares a room, a briefing only reaches some of the team
why.sub: The follow up has to travel to the carer, because the carer cannot travel to the office.

cards.title: Lone working means nobody checks the room
cards.body: In a residential service a manager can look around a group and see who looks lost. In domiciliary care there is no room, and no colleague beside the carer when she has to put new guidance into practice.

cards.title: Reading a message is not understanding it
cards.body: A staff message, a newsletter or a signed note shows what was sent. It does not show whether the carer took in the point, or what she would do alone in a client's home.

cards.title: Chasing eighty carers by phone does not scale
cards.body: Ringing round after a policy change is slow, and it only proves a conversation happened. Without a quick check per carer, gaps stay open until a visit goes wrong.

talk.heading: The questions home care managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: My carers are never together. How can I train them at all?
items.a: You do not need them together. You allocate a short module in the Training screen and each carer finishes it in the Staff Hub, an installable app on her own phone. She can do it before a round, in the car between visits or at home, and you set an optional due date.

items.q: What happens when a carer gets a question wrong?
items.a: It goes into her Follow-up tab in the hub, and she gets an email, at most once a day and in English. She chooses Learn & retry, a short lesson on that exact point followed by a fresh question, or Just retry the same question. She can retry as often as she needs. Nobody has to ring her.

items.q: Can I send a briefing and then check it landed?
items.a: Yes, but it is a manual step. A briefing or a policy change does not trigger anything on its own. You choose the topic module, tick the carers who need it and allocate it. If the briefing was a face to face session, the face to face router for sending a catch up module is on the Professional plan and above.

items.q: Some of my carers speak English as a second language. Does that matter?
items.a: It can. A carer may understand the topic well and still miss a word under pressure. She can open the lesson in her own language, so a wrong answer points to a knowledge gap and not a vocabulary gap. Translation is on the paid plans only.

items.q: What do I see across the team?
items.a: The Knowledge gaps view in Analytics shows open gaps, how many carers are affected, gaps closed in the last 30 days, the most missed questions and the weakest topics. A digest arrives on Monday. Nothing alerts you each time a carer gets a question wrong, so it is a picture to review, not a stream of messages.

items.q: Does this help with domiciliary care compliance and the CQC?
items.a: It gives you a record of what each carer was asked, what she got wrong, the lesson she was given and whether it then landed. That sits alongside the rest of your CQC evidence. It is not a rating or a regulator record, and it does not replace observing a carer's practice.

items.q: Can I try it before I commit?
items.a: Yes. There is a 14 day free trial on the paid plans, and you can create a free account to look around. Ad hoc training is on the paid plans, so check the pricing page for which plan suits your size.

limits.heading: A way to check understanding, not a replacement for watching a carer work

cards.title: It cannot observe practice in a client's home
cards.body: A carer who uses a hoist, gives medication or supports a transfer still needs a competent person to watch her do it. CareStream checks what she knows and keeps the record. It does not see the visit.

cards.title: It does not alert you to every wrong answer
cards.body: The picture reaches you through the Knowledge gaps view and the Monday digest, not as a message each time someone slips. Nothing escalates automatically if a retry is wrong too.

cards.title: Nothing starts on its own, and some parts need a paid plan
cards.body: A briefing does not trigger a module, so you allocate it yourself. Ad hoc training and translation are on the paid plans, and the face to face router is Professional and above. The free plan does not include ad hoc training.

faqs.heading: Domiciliary care training and CareStream, answered

items.q: How do you follow up domiciliary care training when staff work alone?
items.a: Allocate a short module on the topic after the session or the policy change. Each carer completes it on her own phone in the Staff Hub, and a wrong answer goes into her Follow-up tab as a short lesson. You do not need to gather anyone in a room.

items.q: Where does the training come from?
items.a: From your own policies where they cover the topic, with general good practice as the fallback. You pick the topic module, then edit and preview it before you allocate it. You choose the topic, not a single policy or section.

items.q: How soon after a briefing should the check go out?
items.a: Within a few days is a sensible rule: soon enough that the change is fresh, late enough to show what stuck. You choose when to allocate it and you can set a due date. The four question framework helps you decide who needs it.

items.q: What does the CQC expect for domiciliary care training?
items.a: Regulation 18 says staff must receive the appropriate support, training, professional development, supervision and appraisal necessary to carry out the duties they are employed to perform. It does not list courses, so each provider decides what its carers need and must be able to show it.

items.q: How do inspectors look at domiciliary care CQC training evidence?
items.a: The CQC guidance on Regulation 18 says staff should be supervised until they show the competence their role needs, and training needs should be reviewed over time. A record of questions, lessons and results helps show that. See also our guide to staff questions inspectors ask.

No. CareStream is not a pass, a rating or a regulator record. It helps you keep organised evidence of training and follow up, so domiciliary care compliance is something you can show and not only describe. The judgement remains with your manager and the inspector.

guide.heading: A practical way to follow up training in a home care service
guide.lede: Domiciliary care training does not end at the office door. When carers work alone across many homes, the follow up has to be small, quick and easy to do on a phone.

sections.h3: Keep the check short and close to the change
paragraphs: A policy change, a near miss or a refresher briefing is the right moment to check understanding. Keep the check to a few questions on one topic, so a carer can finish it between visits.

Where a point needs hands on practice, such as moving and handling in the home, pair the check with an observed visit. Home specific audits such as home care infection prevention and PPE and home environment and client risk give you a structured way to see practice, not only knowledge.

sections.h3: Four checks that fit a spread out team
checklist: Within a week: allocate a short module on the topic of the briefing or the change, built from your policies.
Whenever an answer is wrong: the carer opens a short lesson on that point, then a fresh question.
Each week: look at the Monday digest and the most missed questions across your rounds.
On the next spot check or supervision: observe one example for any skill that needs hands on practice.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the questions, the lessons and the results together, so you can show understanding as well as attendance, even for carers who were never in the room.
